result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.max_weight_matching()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Find a maximum weight matching in the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L27117-L27211){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.max_weight_matching() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} ![Maximum weight matching](/assets/graphs/max-weight-matching.light.svg){.lightbox fig-alt="The same five-node graph with edge weights. Taking edges by weight, the matching picks 1–2 (5) and 3–4 (4), shown in the accent color with their endpoints. The card shows the returned edge ids 2 and 3, the pairs, and the total weight 5 + 4 = 9." width="100%"} Finds a matching that maximizes the sum of edge weights. Uses a greedy algorithm that selects edges by weight in descending order. For unweighted graphs, all edges have weight `1.0`. Note that this is a greedy approximation, not guaranteed to be optimal for general graphs. For optimal solutions on bipartite graphs, use specialized bipartite matching algorithms. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list[int]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : List of edge IDs forming a maximum weight matching. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Sorts edges by weight in $O(E \log E)$ and admits each into the matching if both endpoints are still free, taking $O(V + E)$ auxiliary space to track the matched set. This greedy scheme is provably optimal on trees and forests but only $\tfrac{1}{2}$-approximate on general graphs (Preis, 1999): a heavy edge that shares an endpoint with two moderately-weighted ones can still be the wrong choice. For an exact optimum on general graphs use Edmonds' weighted blossom algorithm; for bipartite inputs the Hungarian method delivers an exact result in $O(V^3)$. On unweighted graphs every edge scores identically and the call degenerates into `maximal_matching()`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Given a choice between one heavy edge (`A-B`, weight 10) and several light ones, the greedy algorithm grabs the heavy edge first, then fills in the rest of the matching with whatever's left: ::: {#e1222f4f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_node(label="D") .add_edge("A", "B", weight=10.0) .add_edge("B", "C", weight=1.0) .add_edge("C", "D", weight=1.0) .add_edge("A", "C", weight=2.0) ) matching = graph.max_weight_matching() # Returns total weight of the matching (11.0: edges A-B and C-D) sum(graph.get_edge(eid).weight for eid in matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 11.0 ``` ::: ::: For an unweighted graph, every edge has the same implicit weight, so the algorithm just maximizes the number of matched pairs -- here, a complete graph on 8 nodes yields a perfect matching: ::: {#39803d3a .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_full_graph(8) matching = graph.max_weight_matching() # Returns 4 (all 8 nodes paired up) len(matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 4 ``` ::: ::: Being greedy, this can miss the true optimum: in a triangle with a heavy `A-B` edge, the algorithm locks in `A-B` first, leaving `C` unmatched, even though a different weighting could favor a different pair: ::: {#cfadb6c3 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph(weighted=True) .add_node(label="A") .add_node(label="B") .add_node(label="C") .add_edge("A", "B", weight=5.0) .add_edge("B", "C", weight=3.0) .add_edge("A", "C", weight=2.0) ) matching = graph.max_weight_matching() # Returns 1 (only one edge can be chosen in a 3-node graph) len(matching) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 1 ``` ::: :::
